q-4555:
To compute ${f}^{′}(x),$ we first make the substitution $u=\sqrt{x}$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{2}^{\sqrt{x}}\frac{1}{2-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{2}^{u}\frac{1}{2-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

The integrand is continuous on $[2,u],$ and so by FTC II we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{1}{2-{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x})\cdot \frac{1}{2-{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\cdot \frac{1}{2-(\sqrt{x})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}(2-x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-117291:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{x}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{e}^{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{x}^{a}{e}^{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{e}^{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{x}{e}^{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{e}^{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$

The integrand ${e}^{1-{t}^{2}}$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying the FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{x}{e}^{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{e}^{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}{e}^{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{e}^{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-{e}^{1-{x}^{2}}+\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}{e}^{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-{e}^{1-{x}^{2}}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x){e}^{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =-{e}^{1-{x}^{2}}-{e}^{1-{cos}^{2}⁡x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-{e}^{1-{x}^{2}}-{e}^{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$

Finally, we can compute ${f}^{′}(0).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & =-{e}^{1-{0}^{2}}-{e}^{{sin}^{2}⁡0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =-{e}^{1-0}-0 \\  & =-e.\end{aligned}
$$

q-136442:
If a particle moves with constant acceleration $a,$ the position vector of the particle at time $t$ can be found using

$$
r={r}_{0}+ut+\frac{1}{2}a{t}^{2},
$$

 

where ${r}_{0}$ is the initial position of the particle and $u$ is its initial velocity.

In our case, we have

$$
{r}_{0}=0i+0j,\,u=4i+j,\,a=-2i+j.
$$

Therefore, the position vector of the particle after $t=4\,\text{s}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =(0i+0j)+(4i+j)(4)+\frac{1}{2}(-2i+j)(4)^{2} \\  & =(16i+4j)+8(-2i+j) \\  & =(16i+4j)+(-16i+8j) \\  & =12j\,\text{ft}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance from the particle to the origin at this time is

$$
\begin{aligned}|r| & =|12j| \\  & =|12| \\  & =12\,\text{ft}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-50148:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={e}^{3x}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3x}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{3}\,{e}^{3x})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3x}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

q-119038:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =8\int {e}^{-2x}\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2x})+C \\  & =-4{e}^{-2x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-4{e}^{-2x}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =-4(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2x})+Cx+D \\  & =2{e}^{-2x}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

q-71915:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{p}^{′}(t)≈\frac{p(t+h)-p(t)}{h}
$$

at the point $t=0.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=1.$ This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(0) & ≈\frac{p(0+1)-p(0)}{1} \\  & =\frac{p(1)-p(0)}{1} \\  & =5-9 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

q-71921:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{g}^{′}(x)≈\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}{h}
$$

 
at the point $x=1.5.$ Applying the above formula with $x=1.5$ and $h=1$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(1.5) & ≈\frac{g(1.5+1)-g(1.5)}{1} \\  & =\frac{g(2.5)-g(1.5)}{1} \\  & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-47387:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{g}^{′}(x)≈\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}{h}
$$

 
at the point $x=2.$ Applying the above formula with $x=2$ and $h=4$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(2) & ≈\frac{g(2+4)-g(2)}{4} \\  & =\frac{g(6)-g(2)}{4} \\  & =\frac{6-8}{4} \\  & =\frac{-2}{4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-47378:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{s}^{′}(t)≈\frac{s(t+h)-s(t)}{h}
$$

 
at the point $t=6.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{′}(6) & ≈\frac{s(6+2)-s(6)}{2} \\  & =\frac{s(8)-s(6)}{2} \\  & =\frac{20-15}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2} \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So at $t=6$ Andrey's speed is approximately $2.5\,\text{m/s}.$

q-47383:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{W}^{′}(t)≈\frac{W(t+h)-W(t)}{h},
$$

 
at the time $t=1$ with step size $h=2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{W(1+2)-W(1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{W(3)-W(1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{100-50}{2} \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

So, after $1$ minute, the power is increasing at a rate of approximately $25\,\text{watts}/\text{minute}.$

q-77865:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-4,4],$ the function must be continuous on $[-4,4]$ and differentiable on $(-4,4).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function $f(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}}$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[-4,4]$ and differentiable on $(-4,4).$ Therefore, $f(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $g(x)={2}^{1/{x}^{2}}$ is not defined at $x=0,$ hence, it is not continuous at 
$x=0,$ and so it is not continuous on $[-4,4].$ Therefore, $g(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $h(x)=\sqrt{x+4}$ is continuous on $[-4,\infty )$ and differentiable on $(-4,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[-4,4]$ and differentiable on $(-4,4).$ Therefore, $h(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Therefore, only the functions I and III satisfy the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[-4,4].$

q-89347:
The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

$$
x=3\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,t\in [-\pi ,\pi ],\,t\ne \pm \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-hyperbola, we refer to the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14058380/assets/e7ef7fd90c828767359daf69f68f406d61e3f82ad86b1f6b3a9480c99dedadf8.png)

We can see that if we restrict $t$ to $(-\frac{\pi }{2},0],$ we get the quarter-hyperbola.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe the required quarter-hyperbola are

$$
x=3\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},0].
$$

q-106517:
The parametric equations of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by

$$
x=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(\pm a,0).$ From the graph, we have that $(2,0)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=2.$

The asymptotes of a horizontal hyperbola are $y=\pm \frac{b}{a}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are $y=\pm \frac{3}{2}x,$ and so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{b}{a} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{b}{2} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ b & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=2\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

q-47552:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{f}^{′}(x)≈\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h},
$$

 
at the point $x=2.$ Applying the above formula with $x=2$ and $h=4$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & ≈\frac{f(2)-f(2-4)}{4} \\  & =\frac{f(2)-f(-2)}{4} \\  & =\frac{5-1}{4} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-72074:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{f}^{′}(x)≈\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h},
$$

 
at the point $x=3.$ Applying the above formula with $x=3$ and $h=2$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3) & ≈\frac{f(3)-f(3-2)}{2} \\  & =\frac{f(3)-f(1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{0-(-1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-51328:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{h}^{′}(t)≈\frac{h(t)-h(t-h)}{h},
$$

 
at the time $t=3.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(3) & ≈\frac{h(3)-h(3-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{h(3)-h(2)}{1} \\  & =\frac{159-181}{1} \\  & =-22.\end{aligned}
$$

So the rate of change of the altitude is $-22\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$
